opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point should always be the task, not the form. There's a lot of excitement right now about humanoid robots, and I understand why: our world is built for human bodies. Doors, stairs, tools, kitchens, factory lines were all designed around two arms, two legs and a certain height. So if you want one general-purpose machine that can walk into any environment built for people and work there, the humanoid form makes a lot of sense.

But for most specific tasks, the humanoid isn't the most efficient answer. Look at autonomous driving. A self-driving car is a robot, but nobody says it should be a humanoid sitting in the driver's seat turning the wheel. The task is moving people and goods safely on roads, so the form is a vehicle with sensors, compute and actuation built in. In logistics warehouses, wheeled platforms and robotic arms do the job better and more cheaply than legs. In surgery, the robot is a set of very precise, very small instruments. In agriculture it might be a drone or a machine that moves along crop rows.

So I'd describe it as a spectrum. On one end you have highly specialized robots, where the form is optimized for one job and you get the best reliability, cost and safety. On the other end you have general-purpose robots, where the form follows the human environment, and that's where humanoids, or semi-humanoids with wheels and two arms, fit. Many real deployments in the next five to ten years will sit in the middle: a mobile base with dexterous arms, because it's stable, cheaper and good enough for most manipulation.

What has changed is the brain. With large models and embodied AI, the intelligence is becoming more general and more transferable across bodies. That separates the question of form from the question of intelligence. The same foundation model can, in principle, drive a car, a robotic arm or a humanoid, with adaptation. Once intelligence becomes more of a common layer, you can be pragmatic about the body: choose the form that best matches the physics of the task, the cost constraints and the safety requirements.

There's one more factor people sometimes underestimate: the human-robot interaction side. In homes, eldercare or service settings, form also affects trust and acceptance. Sometimes a robot that looks too human creates discomfort, and sometimes a simple, friendly form is better. So the task determines the form, but "task" should include the social context as well as the physical work.

My short answer: form follows function. Use the humanoid where the generality of the human environment really matters, and use specialized forms everywhere else. Over time, I expect a diverse ecosystem of robot bodies sharing increasingly general AI brains.

r001.rationale: The response says specific tasks often call for specialized forms and gives wheeled platforms and robotic arms as better, cheaper options for logistics work, supporting that industrial robots need not be humanoid.

r002.rationale: It discusses household interaction and acceptance but does not express a preference for humanoid form in household robots.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a robot dog or guiding a blind person.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think this is actually one of the most fundamental questions in robotics today, and my view is fairly simple: form should follow function, not the other way around.

If you look at where embodied intelligence is being deployed right now, the vast majority of value is not coming from humanoids. It is coming from robots that look nothing like us. A robotic arm on a factory line, an autonomous vehicle, a warehouse robot that moves shelves, a quadruped inspecting a power station. Each of those forms exists because the task demanded it. A car does not need legs. An arm bolted to a workstation does not need a torso. The environment was already structured, or could be restructured, so the robot could be specialized, and specialization usually means better reliability and lower cost.

So the first principle I would offer is: start from the task and the environment. Ask what degrees of freedom are actually required, what payload, what precision, what duration of operation, and whether the environment can be modified. If the answer is that the environment is fixed and designed for humans, then you begin to have a real argument for a human-like form.

That is the case for humanoids. Our homes, offices, hospitals, stairs, door handles, tools, they were all built around the human body. A general-purpose robot that needs to operate across many of these spaces without redesigning each one benefits from a shape that fits those spaces. The humanoid form is, in a sense, a compatibility layer with the existing human world. And there is a second, often underappreciated reason: data. Humans generate enormous amounts of video of ourselves performing tasks. If the robot shares our morphology, that data transfers much more directly for training.

But I would caution against treating the humanoid as the default answer. Two legs are an expensive, unstable way to move if wheels will do. Five-fingered hands are extraordinarily hard to build and control, and many tasks are better served by a simpler gripper. So I expect the long-term landscape to be plural. We will have specialized forms wherever the task is narrow and the volume is high, and more general, often human-like forms where the task mix is broad and the environment cannot change.

The deeper shift, in my view, is that intelligence is becoming decoupled from form. In the past, the brain and the body of a robot were co-designed and tightly coupled. Now, with foundation models for perception, language, and action, we are moving toward a shared intelligence that can be instantiated in many bodies. That means the question of form becomes much more of an engineering and economic decision rather than an intelligence constraint. And that is a healthy place to be, because it lets us choose the body the task really needs.

r001.rationale: It describes factory-line robotic arms as effective task-specific forms and says they need not resemble humans.

r002.rationale: It says human-like forms can suit homes built around people, but does not express a preference for humanoids in household robots.

r003.rationale: It mentions quadrupeds inspecting power stations, but does not identify a robot dog as sufficient for guiding a blind person.

astra-6.text:
I think you should start with the task, then decide what physical form makes sense. A robot doesn’t necessarily need to look like a human. If its job is to move goods around a warehouse, wheels may be more efficient than legs. If it’s inspecting a pipe, it needs a shape that can move through that space.

The case for a humanoid is stronger when you want one robot to perform many different tasks in an environment designed for people. Our stairs, doors, and tools all assume a human body. Having two hands and two legs can help a robot use that existing infrastructure.

So the question is: What does the robot need to do, and where does it need to operate? The body should follow from that.

r001.rationale: The response says robots need not look human and gives wheels as a more efficient form for moving goods around a warehouse, communicating that industrial tasks do not require a humanoid body.

r002.rationale: It says humanoid form can help when one robot must perform varied tasks in human-designed environments, but does not express a preference for humanoid form in household robots.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a robot dog or guiding a blind person.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with the task: What does the robot need to do, and in what environment? Then you design the physical form around those requirements. If it’s moving goods in a warehouse, wheels may be more efficient than legs. If it needs to work in spaces designed for people, use our tools, or climb stairs, a humanoid form may make sense.

So I don’t think every robot needs to look like a human. The important thing is whether its body helps it perform the task reliably, safely, and efficiently. The form should follow the function.
